subject: Banking
title: Penn Square Bank: Small Bank, Big Damage
description: A fast breakdown of Penn Square Bank: Small Bank, Big Damage for builders.

hook.text: Penn Square Bank was a tiny Oklahoma shopping mall bank.

buildup.text: Penn Square wrote massive energy loans and sold them to bigger banks.

discovery.text: The loans were poorly underwritten. Penn Square's loan officers approved deals on napkins.

twist.text: When Penn Square failed in 1982, the losses cascaded upward.

climax.text: A small bank in a strip mall originated loans that toppled giants. Size doesn't determine systemic risk; connections do.

punchline.text: A shopping mall bank. Loans on napkins. It nearly crashed the system.

quiz.question: Why was Penn Square Bank's failure so damaging?
options: It had sold risky loans to larger banks that also failed

details.summary: Penn Square Bank was a tiny Oklahoma shopping mall bank that triggered a chain reaction of major bank failures in 1982 by originating billions in risky oil loans and selling participations to Continental Illinois and other large institutions.
details.whyItMatters: Penn Square proved that a small bank can cause systemic damage by selling its risks upstream to larger institutions. The failure demonstrated how interconnected banking creates hidden vulnerabilities across the system.
takeaways: Penn Square had just $525 million in assets but originated billions in loan participations
Its failure directly caused Continental Illinois to need a government rescue
Oil price declines turned the bank's speculative energy loans into massive losses

faq.question: How did a small bank cause such widespread damage?
faq.answer: Penn Square originated far more loans than it could hold, selling participations to major banks including Continental Illinois and Seattle-First. When the loans defaulted, the losses rippled through every bank that had purchased them.

faq.question: What lesson does Penn Square offer about banking risk?
faq.answer: Penn Square showed that risk in banking is about connections, not just size. A small institution can poison the system if larger banks blindly purchase its risks. Due diligence on loan quality must happen at every level of the chain.
